PYTHON / REGRESSION / MODEL COMPARISON

Wine quality.
Testing the prediction.

Can chemical measurements estimate a sensory quality score? A comparison of regression models, with an honest look at generalisation and the limits of the experiment.

At a glance.

Context
Portfolio modelling project · 2024
My contribution
Feature preparation, regression comparisons and interpretation of training/test performance.
Main evidence
The tuned Random Forest records a test MAE of 0.558 score points in saved outputs.
Evidence boundary
Saved notebook results; source data and trained artifacts are not bundled.

6,497 initial records · red and white wine · 1,168 exact duplicates removed · 5,329 records before missing-value filtering. Results are extracted from saved notebook outputs; the source CSV and trained artifacts are absent from the repository. No fresh training run is claimed.

The question and my work.

I explored physicochemical measurements such as acidity, sulphur dioxide, density and alcohol, then prepared features and compared regression models for the recorded sensory score. The workflow includes duplicate removal, missing-value filtering, train/test splitting, outlier capping, encoding, scaling, cross-validation and hyperparameter search.

Analytical goal

Assess whether measurements contain useful predictive signal and compare errors across model families. Quality is an ordinal sensory rating; regression treats differences between scores as numeric distances.

Potential use

A validated model might help prioritise samples for human review. This project does not establish production readiness, better fermentation outcomes or increased sales, and the score should not replace sensory assessment.

INTERACTIVE / SAVED MODEL RESULTS

Compare error, not just a headline score.

Loading saved model results…

Select a model to inspect both training and test values. Source tables: notebook cells 136 and 158. The initial table labels sklearn GradientBoostingRegressor as “XGBoost”; this page corrects that label. Tuned XGBoost uses XGBRegressor, so these are different algorithms rather than a clean before/after pair.

The result

Tuned Random Forest has the lowest saved test MAE among the five tuned models: 0.558 score points, with R² 0.346. Its training MAE is 0.204 and R² is 0.909. That gap warrants investigation; it does not support calling the model free of overfitting.

What MAE means

An MAE of 0.558 means an average absolute error of roughly half a score point on this test sample. It is not 55.8% accuracy. R² describes performance relative to predicting the test target mean; it is not a classification accuracy either.

Understand the target first.

Of the 5,329 deduplicated records, 2,327 have score 6 and only five have score 9. Overall error can therefore hide poor predictions at the extremes. The notebook’s type chart uses 3,970 white and 1,359 red records; its commentary reverses the types and incorrectly implies market popularity. These are sample proportions only.

Evaluation choices that matter.

  1. Holdout: the main train/test split is 70/30 with random state 46. Exact duplicates are removed before splitting; missing-feature rows are excluded.
  2. Feature preparation: capping, scaling and encoding are fitted on training data. Cross-validation and grid search then use the already transformed training matrix, so preprocessing should move inside each fold for a cleaner estimate.
  3. Model search: five-fold searches optimise negative MAE. sklearn’s negative scoring convention is not a negative error; closer to zero is better.
  4. Selection: the notebook compares and selects models using test results. A final untouched test set or nested evaluation is needed to reduce selection optimism.

Limitations & next improvements.

What remains uncertain

  • Saved outputs were reviewed, not reproduced from the missing CSV.
  • No production batch, winery or future-vintage validation is demonstrated.
  • Rare scores have little support; average metrics need per-score breakdowns.
  • The notebook’s causal production and market recommendations exceed the observed features and study design.

The next iteration

  1. Package the data provenance, dependency versions and a single end-to-end preprocessing pipeline.
  2. Add mean/median DummyRegressor baselines, fold-local preprocessing and repeated or nested evaluation.
  3. Inspect residuals by quality and wine type; report uncertainty and out-of-range inputs.
  4. Validate on genuinely new batches before testing any decision-support use.
